newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: SOCCER-FEATURE-Argentine hero Maradona fading out in sleaze and drugs.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FEATURE-Argentine hero Maradona fading out in sleaze and drugs.

text.p: In the 20 years since a hungry 15-year old with a mop of black curls made his debut in first-division soccer, Diego Maradona has arguably tasted more glory and more disgrace than any other modern sportsman.

That first game in October 1976 for Argentinos Juniors against Talleres de Cordoba ended in defeat, despite young Maradona's dazzling performance; now his career looks like it is fading out the same way, in a blur of drugs, sleaze and bitterness.

"These boys never really escape from the slums," sneered an ageing upper-class peroxide blonde who asked that her name not be used, discussing a scandal that has monopolised conversation in Argentina for nearly a month -- the arrest of Maradona's manager and close friend, Guillermo Coppola, on cocaine-dealing charges.

It is easy to sneer at Maradona. He weeps in public for Coppola and admits he is a cocaine addict himself and takes part in wild parties featuring drugs and women half his age. He is overweight and has not played for his team, Buenos Aires' Boca Juniors, for nearly three months.

The star of Argentina's 1986 World Cup victory said this week his new ambition was to retire from soccer and interview Cuban leader Fidel Castro, whom he greatly admires. "I have an enormous desire to fly off to Cuba and conduct the first interview with the commander," he told an interviewer.

Maradona changes his mind about retiring more often than he changes his bizarre hairdos, switching from a yellow stripe to a pony tail. But he panted "I haven't got the strength" after a rare training session on Oct. 30, the day he turned 36 -- "the saddest birthday of my life."

Maradona's loyalty to his 49-year-old playboy manager, blamed by many Argentines for his drug habit, is touching. Police found a pound (400 grams) of cocaine in a flower pot at Coppola's home three weeks ago. But Maradona naively argues: "Guillermo didn't have time to be a dealer because he was with me all the time, from eight in the morning till 12 at night."

He alleges "dark political interests" were behind the arrest and accuses friends in powerful places, who once included President Carlos Menem, his late son Carlitos and his private secretary Ramon Hernandez, of abandoning him. "My phone used to ring every 15 seconds but suddenly it's not ringing any more," said Maradona, who only last summer was asked by Menem to lead his "Sun Without Drugs" campaign.
Maradona is so bitter at Menem and the Peronist Party establishment that he now confesses to "regret giving anything to Argentina, though not to ordinary Argentines."

Through thick and thin, ordinary Argentines still idolise Maradona, much as they idolised the late world champion boxer Carlos Monzon even after he was jailed for killing his wife. They portray Maradona as the victim of his own success.

Their loyalty was clear at the Buenos Aires courthouse where he went to give evidence in Coppola's trial. Court staff were reprimanded for mobbing and cheering Maradona and posing with him for photos, and the front-page headline on Argentina's top-selling newspaper Clarin the next day read: "The Witness We Love Most."

Clarin journalist Miguel Angel Bertolotto marked the 20th anniversary of Maradona's debut with a misty-eyed recollection of the game. "He looked like a little wet chick, sitting on a rough wooden bench in the darkest corner of the old changing room. He had a kid's face, his bright eyes were full of wonder, his head covered in black curls and his voice almost inaudible."

"I could tell right away we were in the presence of one of the greatest players in Argentine football," recalls then Argentine coach Cesar Luis Menotti, who two years later left the rising star off Argentina's victorious World Cup team.
Maradona went on to play four World Cups, captaining the team that won the 1986 World Cup final against Germany and crying when they lost to Germany in the 1990 finals in Italy.

Scandal erupted the following year with a 15-month ban for failing a dope test. Then Coppola was charged with drug-dealing and soon afterwards Maradona was arrested in Buenos Aires for possession of cocaine.
Two blinding games in the 1994 World Cup sparked talk of a revival, but he failed another drug test after a game against Nigeria and was banned from playing for another 15 months.

He tried coaching without success, shot reporters with an air rifle and offered surreal excuses for his drug ban, even saying the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency secretly drugged Catholic communion wafers before a game because Maradona was "involved in drugs and defended Fidel Castro."
That year, Brazil's Pele offered him $6 million to play for Santos, but Coppola sabotaged the deal and signed him for the Buenos Aires team instead.

"Sadly, it's common for stars to keep bad company and that's what I thought when this man appeared," Pele told the Brazilian press recently. "Time proved me right, for now this man's in jail and I don't know if Diego will ever play again."

Meanwhile Maradona has ventured into movies, playing himself in "The Day Maradona Met Gardel," a bizarre fantasy that has him saving Argentine 1920s tango idol Carlos Gardel from singing for eternity.

Calling Maradona "one of those people who make the world a better place," writer Alejandro Dolina, his co-star in the film, added: "But we all had the feeling he was going to disappear at any moment. A professional footballer's time always runs out."
